We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-193)
response:
Activation steering works by adding a vector to a model's residual stream at some layer to shift its behavior — the central question is whether the directions learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at one layer constitute a stable, interpretable basis that can be reliably manipulated, or whether the geometry of these feature directions is entangled in ways that make clean steering impossible. SAEs decompose activations into sparse combinations of learned features, but those features are defined layer-locally: there's no guarantee that a "anger" direction at layer 12 points anywhere coherent relative to a "anger" direction at layer 20, because the residual stream rotates and compounds across layers. The cross-layer interference problem is that steering vectors injected at layer L don't stay put — they propagate forward through attention and MLP sublayers, getting projected, rotated, and mixed with everything else in the stream, so a vector that's sparse and clean in one SAE's basis may be dense and incoherent in the next layer's basis. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses: superposition. Beginners assume SAE features are roughly orthogonal, but models represent far more features than dimensions by packing them into near-orthogonal directions in high-dimensional space — meaning a steering vector almost certainly has nonzero dot products with dozens of other features, and those ghost activations compound as the vector propagates, causing side-effects that are invisible in single-layer analysis. The deeper worry is that cross-layer SAE dictionaries may not be commensurable at all — you may be comparing apples to bicycles when you try to track a "feature" across layers.

Since the MLP nonlinearity is the primary sparsity-destroyer, does it follow that steering vectors injected between the MLP and the next attention layer — i.e., after the nonlinearity has already acted — should degrade more gracefully, and if so, why don't standard steering protocols exploit this?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-195)
response:
The intuition is partially correct but has a hidden catch: injecting after the MLP output means the vector enters the residual stream at a point where the next layer's MLP hasn't yet acted, so you get one clean linear pass through the next attention sublayer before hitting another nonlinearity — attention is purely linear in the value-weighted output, so your vector propagates through it without sparsity destruction, just a learned linear mixing. This means post-MLP injection does buy you one more linear transformation before the next blowup, which is genuinely better than injecting mid-MLP. But the reason standard protocols don't exploit this is partly sociological and partly technical: the canonical steering vector literature (Zou et al.'s "Representation Engineering," 2023; Turner et al.'s activation addition work) was developed by finding directions in residual stream activations at token positions, and the residual stream is most naturally accessed at layer boundaries — pre- and post-layernorm checkpoints are where frameworks like TransformerLens expose activations by default, so that's where people steer. The deeper technical issue is that "after MLP, before attention" is not a stable semantic checkpoint: attention at layer L+1 reads from all positions via Q/K/V projections, meaning your injected vector at one position gets mixed with every other token's representation, and the mixing weights (the attention pattern) are themselves a function of the very activations you just modified — so you've introduced a feedback loop that's hard to analyze. What would actually help is injecting into the value vectors of specific attention heads rather than the residual stream, which would let you route influence through only the heads you want — this is closer to what path patching (Wang et al., IOI paper, 2022) does mechanistically, but that technique is diagnostic rather than a steering protocol. The gap is that nobody has built a steering protocol that treats attention heads as addressable write targets rather than using the blunt instrument of residual stream addition.

The convolution framing is essentially correct with one precision fix: it's not the steered token's outgoing attention that matters but rather how much other tokens attend to it — the steered position's modified residual gets written into other positions weighted by the attention scores those positions assign to the steered token, so the effective spread is governed by the steered token's column in the attention matrix, not its row. This means a steered token that is heavily attended to — a period, a separator token, or what Elhage et al. (2021) called "memory" tokens that aggregate information — will broadcast its perturbation broadly, while a steered token in a position that other tokens ignore will contain the perturbation locally. Empirically this predicts that steering the BOS token or other high-attention-sink positions (identified in Xiao et al.'s "Efficient Streaming Language Models," 2023, which quantified attention sinks) should produce the most globally distributed effect, and anecdotally practitioners do report that steering early tokens or delimiter tokens produces stronger behavioral shifts — but this hasn't been rigorously measured as a function of attention column mass. The consequence for effectiveness is asymmetric: broad broadcasters make steering more potent but less controllable, because the perturbation lands on every downstream token regardless of semantic relevance; narrow tokens give surgical control but weak global effect, which may be why single-token steering often requires large coefficient magnitudes to produce behavioral change. There's a further compounding effect: after layer L+1 attention mixes the vector, each recipient token runs it through their MLP at L+1, so the sparsity blowup problem now fires in parallel across all positions that received nonzero weight, and the resulting dense garbage accumulates in each token's residual stream independently. This implies an underappreciated interaction: the optimal injection site isn't just a function of layer depth and MLP position, but of the joint distribution of attention patterns and MLP feature geometry at that layer — a quantity nobody has mapped systematically.

prompt:
Since attention sinks accumulate perturbations from steered tokens and then rebroadcast them, could adversarial steering exploit this by deliberately targeting sink tokens to achieve disproportionate model-wide influence — and what would a principled defense against that look like?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-197)
response:
Yes, this is a real and underappreciated attack surface: if you can inject a perturbation into a token position that functions as an attention sink — BOS, delimiter tokens, or the period tokens that Xiao et al. quantified as absorbing 20-30% of total attention mass in some layers — you get a multiplicative amplification effect where a small vector addition propagates to nearly every subsequent token's residual stream before the next MLP fires. The adversarial version of this is essentially already present in prompt injection attacks, but without the mechanistic framing: a carefully crafted token sequence that becomes an attention sink (by virtue of its position or content) could carry a steering payload that spreads model-wide, and the attacker's leverage scales with the sink's attention mass rather than the raw magnitude of the injected vector. Concretely, you'd want to solve for a token embedding (or soft prompt vector) that simultaneously maximizes attention drawn from all other positions and has high dot product with the encoder directions of features you want to activate in the next layer's SAE — a bicriteria optimization that hasn't been published but is straightforwardly differentiable given white-box access. A principled defense has to operate at one of three choke points: prevent the sink from forming (hard, because attention sinks emerge from training dynamics and suppressing them degrades performance, as StreamingLLM showed by needing to preserve sinks to maintain coherence); detect anomalous perturbation of known sink positions at inference time; or make the value projection at sink positions low-rank so that whatever gets written there has limited expressivity when rebroadcast. The third option is the most tractable and maps onto existing work on attention head ablation and rank reduction (Voita et al., 2019 showed many heads are prunable without loss), but it hasn't been framed explicitly as a defense against steering amplification via sinks. The deeper structural problem is that attention sinks exist because the model learned to use them as a computational primitive for global context aggregation — so any defense that degrades the sink also degrades the legitimate computation it supports, and you can't easily separate the two without interpretability tools fine-grained enough to distinguish "legitimate global context" from "adversarial payload," which brings you right back to needing reliable cross-layer SAE decomposition.

response:
The coherence problem is sharp: a standard SAE is trained on the activation vector at a single token position and implicitly assumes that vector encodes something about that token's semantic content — but a sink token's activation is dominated by what other tokens have written into it via attention, making it a weighted superposition of context-dependent information from the entire sequence, with the weighting changing for every new input. This means SAE features learned on sink positions would be interpretable only in a relational sense — not "this feature means X" but "this feature activates when the global context contains pattern Y," which is a fundamentally different and much harder concept to validate with standard per-feature interpretability metrics like maximum activating dataset examples. Anthropic's April 2024 SAE work (Gao et al.) trained SAEs on residual stream activations across positions but didn't disaggregate by positional role — sink vs. non-sink — so we don't actually know empirically whether sink-position SAEs learn coherent features or dense contextual hash-like representations. There's a theoretical argument that they could be interpretable in a compressed-sensing sense: if the model uses the sink to store a sparse summary of global context (analogous to a soft key-value memory), then the SAE might recover those summary dimensions as features, but this requires the model to have learned to write sparse summaries into the sink, which is an assumption about training dynamics nobody has verified. The deeper incoherence is that "local interpretability" presupposes you can understand a feature by looking at individual activations in isolation, but sink token features are inherently defined by their relationship to a distribution over contexts — their meaning is an emergent property of the attention pattern that populated them, which varies per sequence and can't be recovered from the activation vector alone without knowing the full context. This suggests that SAE-based interpretability may need a fundamentally different paradigm for sink positions: something like a conditional feature dictionary where features are indexed not just by activation direction but by the attention pattern that produced them.
